title: Connexins are essential for the contribution of latent progenitors to healing after spinal cord injury
authors: Falco, M. V.; Fabbiani, G.; Prieto, D.; Vidal, M.; Benitez, M.; Rehermann, M. I.; Silvera, C.; Simeone, R.; Trigo, F. F.; Russo, R. E.
abstract: Gap junctions are important regulators of the biology of neural stem cells. Both in vertebrates with regenerative abilities and neonatal rodents, ependymal cells communicate via connexin (Cx) 43 and Cx26. Gap junction coupling and Cx26 are down-regulated as the ependyma becomes quiescent in adulthood, but injury overrules this developmental down-regulation suggesting a role for Cx signaling in the reactivation of ependymal cells. However, direct evidence of the involvement of these Cxs in the reactivation of the ependymal stem cell niche is lacking. Here, we aim to explore the role of Cx26 and Cx43 in the response of ependymal cells to injury by means of specific genetic deletion. We find that Cx26 is critical for the proliferative response of ependymal cells to injury. The reduced response of ependymal cells by Cx26 deletion increased the extension of the lesion because of impaired healing resulting from a weak contribution of the ependymal stem cell niche. On the other hand, Cx43 -via gap junction coupling and hemichannels- plays a key role in the communication of Ca2+ signals between ependymal cells induced by activation of P2X7 receptors. Our data show that Cxs are relevant targets to manipulate the ependymal stem cell niche to achieve better healing after spinal cord injury.

title: Sequential coupling of sleep oscillations enables concept-neuron reactivation and supports information flow across the human hippocampal-cortical circuit
authors: Schwimmbeck, F.; Niediek, J.; Borger, V.; Surges, R.; Trinka, E.; Schreiner, T.; Mormann, F.
abstract: Effective memory consolidation during sleep is thought to rely on the transfer of reactivated memory traces from the hippocampus to the cortex. However, the mechanisms supporting this essential dialogue across brain areas remain poorly understood. Here, we recorded single-neuron activity (n = 1097) in the medial temporal lobe (MTL) of 10 epilepsy patients across 21 nights of sleep. Before sleep, patients engaged in a memory task with stimuli eliciting concept-neuron responses. During non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, neuronal firing locked to sharp wave-ripples (SWR) revealed a directed flow of information from the hippocampus to cortical targets. Notably, within SWR-driven activity, experience-dependent concept neurons exhibited elevated co-activation both within and across MTL regions, indicating selective reactivation of behaviorally relevant information. Cross-regional co-activation of concept cells was markedly enhanced when hippocampal SWRs coincided with cortical slow oscillation-spindle complexes, suggesting an active role of the cortex in shaping interregional communication. These findings provide evidence that SWRs in humans selectively reactivate experience-related neural ensembles across the hippocampal-cortical network, while synergistic interactions with cortical slow oscillation-spindle events might facilitate effective memory consolidation.

title: A non-invasive approach to study localized forced in 3D epithelia
authors: Gouirand, N.; Ibrahimi, M.; Valotteau, C.; Lecouffe, B.; Le Bivic, A.; Massey Harroche, D.; Rico, F.; Merkel, M.; Delacour, D.; Bazellieres, E.
abstract: Epithelial tissue integrity and remodelling rely on mechanical coupling between cytoskeletal organization and adhesion complexes, but their orchestration in three-dimensional (3D) epithelia remains unresolved. Here, we introduced a non-invasive strategy to locally probe forces within 3D epithelial tissues. We engineered elastic polyacrylamide (PAAm) microbeads with cell-like size and mechanical properties, enabling their integration into tissues. PAAm microbeads were spontaneously engulfed by the tissue, establishing an intrinsic interface. This allowed bead deformation to be directly correlated with local cytoskeletal architecture and adhesion organization, visualized through high-resolution imaging and quantitative 3D computational reconstruction. Using this approach, we demonstrated that localized mechanical perturbations trigger cytoskeletal remodelling while preserving tissue polarity. We further identified extracellular matrix composition as a key determinant of bead-tissue interactions. At the bead-cell interface, cells assembled tension-bearing focal adhesions and actin stress fibers. Quantitative analysis of bead deformation revealed sub-cellular scale patterns of cell-bead interaction forces, which correlated with the localization of cytoskeletal elements. Our findings extend previous traction force microscopy observations to 3D, revealing coordinated, spatially heterogeneous forces specifically at the cell-bead interface. Taken together, this enabled us to dissect the interplay between cellular processes and tissue mechanics in a non-invasive way in 3D model systems.

title: Comparative genomics of zooxanthellate and azooxanthellate Palythoa (Cnidaria: Zoantharia) provides insights into symbiosis evolution and the origin of palytoxin
authors: Yoshioka, Y.; Shoguchi, E.; Chiu, Y.-L.; Kawamitsu, M.; Reimer, J. D.; Yamashita, H.
abstract: Zoantharians (Cnidaria) are globally distributed from shallow reefs to the deep sea, yet their genomic resources remain scarce. Within the zoantharian genus Palythoa, most species harbor photosymbiotic dinoflagellates, whereas some have secondarily lost this symbiosis, allowing genomic changes associated with symbiotic status to be examined. Palythoa is also the original source of palytoxin, one of the most potent marine toxins known, but whether it is produced by the host or by associated microorganisms remains unresolved. Here we generated high-quality genome assemblies of two zooxanthellate Palythoa species and compared five Palythoa genomes spanning both symbiotic states with those of other anthozoans. Across anthozoans, genome size scaled with transposable element content, particularly retrotransposons. The azooxanthellate lineage carries substitutions in conserved domains of the symbiosis-related proteins LePin and NPC2 and shows rapid evolution of the lectin gene CLEC4A, whereas NF-{kappa}B and V-type H+-ATPase remain conserved. Palythoa genomes showed no lineage-specific expansion of polyketide synthase (PKS) genes; cnidarian PKS genes were restricted to P. caribaeorum and P. sp. sakurajimensis (clade III). In contrast, 27 bacterial PKS sequences were recovered from metatranscriptomes and a metagenome-assembled genome across species, including an azooxanthellate species, indicating that they derive from associated bacterial rather than Symbiodiniaceae. These genomes provide a comparative framework for zoantharians and reveal genomic changes associated with symbiotic status. We propose that palytoxin originates from associated bacteria rather than from the host, a hypothesis that can be tested by identifying the producing bacteria and their biosynthetic gene clusters.

title: From Arm to Leg: A Shared Primitive Framework for Solving Inverse Kinematics in Human Movement
abstract: In motor control, the idea of a modular control architecture has been repeatedly discussed. This framework has been widely applied to kinematic and kinetic data, primarily to examine how the central nervous system (CNS) controls multiple elements simultaneously and how it handles redundant or excessive degrees of freedom. However, the inverse kinematics problem, traditionally defined as the mapping from a desired task-space outcome to the corresponding joint-space solution, has usually been treated separately from this framework. Recent work from our laboratory suggests that modular control may directly address all these problems by relying on a shared low-dimensional primitive space common to internal and external movement representations, as supported by recent studies of human hand-drawing kinematics. In the present study, we extended this framework from upper-limb drawing to lower-limb gait kinematics. We also used it to explore how different CNS pathologies may alter the organization of movement within this shared space. Overall, this study investigates whether walking, like other forms of movement, can be understood as arising from a small number of underlying primitives that are flexibly combined across coordinate systems.

title: Rapid experience-dependent tuning of spinal and transcortical stretch reflexes supports goal-directed movement
authors: Akter, T.; Rohlen, R.; Petersson, P.; Dimitriou, M.
abstract: The short-latency stretch reflex (SLR) is the fastest sensorimotor response in human limbs. The spinal SLR scales with background muscle activity and is affected by recent movement history. But adaptive plasticity of spinal reflexes has classically been studied through operant conditioning, which induces an arbitrary change in reflex size over days to weeks. In contrast, rapid, experience-dependent feedback adaptation is often attributed to transcortical mechanisms underlying the long-latency reflex (LLR). Whether task constraints can progressively shape the SLR within a single session remains unclear. Here, naive human adults (n = 16; 9 females, 7 males) performed an instructed-delay reaching task while holding a robotic manipulandum which delivered brief haptic perturbations during action preparation. We recorded high-density surface electromyography (64-channel arrays) from the pectoralis major and posterior deltoid to investigate reflex gains. Pre-perturbation muscle activity showed no systematic goal-directed change. With a long-enough preparatory delay (750 ms), SLR gains decreased progressively with experience when the planned movement was expected to stretch the homonymous muscle, rather than shorten it. This tuning occurred in both muscles, was evident within individual participants, and was accompanied by a corresponding decrease in reflexively generated force opposing perturbations toward the cued target. No such tuning was detected with a short preparatory delay (250 ms). LLR responses were goal-directed from the first trial blocks and progressed in a comparable manner across the session, at both preparatory delays. Our study shows that spinal feedback circuits can progressively adapt within a single session to support the performance of goal-directed movements.

title: Histone modifications directly modulate transcription factor binding to nucleosomes
abstract: Transcription factors (TFs) that can recognize specific DNA sequences within nucleosomes play key roles in regulating cell fate transitions, but what regulates their condition-dependent binding to nucleosomes remains poorly understood. Here, we determined the direct effects of H3K27ac, H3K27me3 and H3K9me3 on binding by 7 human TFs to a highly diverse library of nucleosomes. We found that these marks influence the preference of FOXA1 and PAX7 to bind as monomers versus dimers to nucleosomes. Furthermore, H3K27ac impairs TF binding at internal regions of nucleosomes, enhancing end-binding preferences, for most of the assayed TFs. Our results suggest that histone marks represent an additional layer of cis-regulatory encoding that directly regulates TF interactions with nucleosomal binding sites.

title: Aβ42-Driven α-synuclein Fibril Polymorphism and Distinct Intracellular Aggregation
authors: Saha, P.; Liyanaarachchige, T.; Alim, A.; Paek, J.; Lee, M.
abstract: The frequent coexistence of -synuclein (-syn) and amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}) aggregates in neurodegenerative diseases suggests that heterotypic interactions between these amyloidogenic proteins may influence disease progression, yet their molecular consequences remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated how distinct aggregation states of A{beta}42, monomers and preformed fibrils (PFFs), modulate -syn fibril formation, structure, and downstream neuronal pathology. Thioflavin T kinetics showed that A{beta}42 monomers delayed -syn fibril formation, whereas A{beta}42 PFFs exhibited a trend toward accelerated aggregation, indicating aggregation state-dependent effects on -syn aggregation. Negative-stain TEM, proteinase K digestion, and solid-state NMR spectroscopy further demonstrated that both A{beta}42 monomers and PFFs altered -syn fibril structure, generating distinct fibril conformations depending on the A{beta}42 concentration and aggregation state. To determine whether these conformational differences influence pathological activity, -syn PFF variants generated in the presence of different concentrations of A{beta}42 monomers or PFFs were applied to dopaminergic neuronal cells. -Syn fibrils formed in the presence of A{beta}42 PFFs showed greater capacity to induce intraneuronal -syn aggregation than -syn PFFs, whereas fibrils formed in the presence of A{beta}42 monomers exhibited similar or reduced seeding capacity relative to -syn PFFs. Together, our findings demonstrate that heterotypic interactions with A{beta}42 reshape -syn aggregation pathways and fibril conformations, generating structurally distinct -syn fibril populations with different neuronal seeding activities. These results provide a molecular framework for understanding how cross-talk between amyloidogenic proteins may contribute to structural and pathological heterogeneity in mixed neurodegenerative diseases.

title: The mannose 6-phosphate receptor system is ancient, widespread in eukaryotes, and functionally diversified in the human parasite Trichomonas vaginalis
authors: Shinde, A. P.; Kaur, H.; Guu, S.-Y.; Zdrha, A.; Smutna, T.; Rada, P.; Harant, K.; Khoo, K.-H.; Dacks, J. B.; Tachezy, J.
abstract: In mammals, the mannose 6-phosphate (M6P) pathway tags newly synthesized hydrolases for delivery to the lysosomes. The pathway underlies healthy lysosomal function, but whether an equivalent system operates outside animals remains largely unexplored. Surveying 53 representative species, across eukaryotic supergroups we show that the M6P receptor (MPR), the phosphorylating enzyme GNPT, and the uncovering enzyme (UCE) form a statistically robust, co-occurring module across extant eukaryotic supergroups. In the human parasite Trichomonas vaginalis, this module has diversified into an expanded MPR family of seven paralogs, the largest reported within these 53 species, alongside a structurally minimal single GNPT gene, despite the complete absence of UCE. Using co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP), mass spectrometry and confocal microscopy, we demonstrate that MPRs and GNPT localise to the Golgi apparatus, and their interactomes show paralog-specific enrichment of distinct hydrolase cargo, adaptor complexes and the retromer complex proteins for retrieval of MPRs, presenting a full receptor-recycling cycle. Critically, mass spectrometry based glycomics directly detects mature M6P-modified N-glycans in T. vaginalis built on unique Man5GlcNAc2 structure with no trace of GlcNAc-capped intermediate, seen in mammalian cells. Together, these results provide evidence that M6P pathway is an ancient and widespread eukaryotic system, with its functionally diversified variant operating in T. vaginalis for lysosomal biogenesis.

title: Scarless regeneration requires post-translational proteolytic regulation via macrophage-derived Legumain
authors: Mo, J.; Levitz, H.; Ali, S.; Lee, S.; Sherwood, D.; Anderson, T.; Spack, K.; Blumenkrantz, M.; Weinstein, E.; Smeeton, J.
abstract: Macrophages express proteolytic factors in response to injury but how proteases are deployed and regulated during regeneration are incompletely defined. Beyond their transcriptomic expression, activity of individual proteases is defined both by their unique substrate specificity and post-translational modifications of their active forms. Here we show a key role for the lysosomal protease Legumain in controlling ECM dynamics and post-translational processing of the regenerative proteome. Injury interface-targeted Ctsla localization and post-translational processing requires Lgmn in macrophages. Extracellular cues from physical remodeling control differentiation state and injury response of ligament resident fibroblasts. Loss of ECM turnover, including localized Fibronectin 1a/b remodeling, impairs dedifferentiation in legumain mutants and leads to fibrotic scarring. Taken together, we demonstrate a role for macrophage-derived lysosomal proteases as specialized tools required to fine-tune proteome composition and function in regeneration.

title: BeatRatePy - Automated Hight-Throughput Python-Based Beat Rate Quantification and Generation of Speed and Contraction Traces
authors: Held, M.; Partington, W.; Waring, T.; Dev, A.; Isherwood, L.; Boulton, B.; Sharma, P.; Herbert, R.; Kudoh, T.; Corbett, A. D.; Burton, R. A. B.
abstract: Analysing cardiac motion from label free imaging can be difficult, especially when recordings vary in quality or show complex movement. We developed a Python-based pipeline that automatically measures beat rate, contraction, speed from transmitted light timelapse data. The workflow runs in a Jupyter notebook and uses straightforward steps that can be followed easily, making the analysis accessible including to users with limited coding experience. Using human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes imaged on a Zeiss Cell Discoverer 7, the pipeline produced beat rates, contraction and contraction speed measurements that matched expected behaviour. To test wider use, we applied the same workflow to killifish larvae heart recordings and public datasets, changing only basic input parameters. The pipeline performed consistently across these different systems and did not require changes to the underlying code. By supporting clear parameter control and use across laboratories, microscopy platforms and repositories, this approach strengthens reproducible analysis of cardiac motion from label free imaging.

title: Generation of an induced pluripotent stem cell line, LCSBi021-A, from a Parkinson's disease patient harboring the missense mutation c.213C>G (p.Ser71Arg) in the RAB32 gene
authors: Boumpoureka, I.; Gorgogietas, V.; Petkovski, E.; Halder, R.; Massart, F.; NCER-PD Consortium,  ; Krueger, R.
abstract: Dermal fibroblasts were obtained from a 40-year-old male patient with Parkinson's disease (PD), harboring the c.213C>G (p.Ser71Arg) variant in the RAB32 gene. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) were generated using the CytoTune-iPS 2.0 Sendai Reprogramming Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The presence of the c.213C>G base exchange in exon 1 of RAB32 was confirmed by Next Generation Sequencing. The iPSCs are free of genomically integrated reprogramming genes, express pluripotency markers, display in vitro differentiation potential into all three germ layers and exhibit karyotypic integrity. Our iPSC line is available for research purposes to dissect molecular mechanisms of neurodegeneration in PD.
